title: Why can @Transactional(readOnly=true) cause an INSERT or UPDATE to silently disappear with no error? Explain how FlushMode.MANUAL means Hibernate never flushes pending changes, how a class-level readOnly setting is inherited by a write method, and how to fix it so writes are never silently dropped.
shortTitle: How does readOnly=true silently drop writes?
keyPoints: @Transactional(readOnly=true) tells Spring to set Hibernate's flush mode to FlushMode.MANUAL
In MANUAL flush mode, Hibernate never automatically flushes pending changes to the database
Any INSERT or UPDATE queued in the persistence context is silently discarded at commit -- no exception
Class-level readOnly=true is inherited by all methods, including write methods
A write method under inherited readOnly silently becomes a no-op for database changes
Fix: override with @Transactional(readOnly=false) or plain @Transactional on every write method
readOnly is a correctness switch disguised as a performance optimization -- treat it with care

s1_definition.oneliner: @Transactional(readOnly=true) switches Hibernate to manual flush mode, which silently discards all pending INSERT and UPDATE statements with no error -- never let a write method inherit a class-level readOnly.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **readOnly hint** -- when set to `true`, Spring passes a read-only hint down to the JDBC connection (`Connection.setReadOnly(true)`) and to the Hibernate session.
- **FlushMode.MANUAL** -- Spring changes the Hibernate session's flush mode from AUTO to MANUAL. In MANUAL mode, Hibernate will not automatically flush the persistence context before queries or at commit time.
- **Silent discard** -- any entity modification or `save()` call under readOnly is held in the persistence context but never flushed to the database. The pending SQL is discarded when the transaction commits. No exception is thrown.
- **Class-level inheritance** -- a `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` annotation on the class is inherited by all methods. A write method that does not override the annotation silently loses its writes.
- **Fix** -- explicitly annotate every write method with `@Transactional` or `@Transactional(readOnly = false)` to restore FlushMode.AUTO.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the supervisor gives the entire department an "inquiry only" stamp for the day (class-level readOnly). Any transfer form filled out by a teller is accepted and looks normal, but the vault silently throws it in the bin because the department is stamped "inquiry only." Rajesh walks away thinking Rs.50,000 moved, but nothing happened. The fix: the transfer counter gets its own "full access" stamp (method-level @Transactional) that overrides the department stamp.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  FlushMode.AUTO (default, readOnly=false)                 │
│                                                           │
│  Entity modified → dirty flag set                         │
│       │                                                   │
│  Before query or commit:                                  │
│       │                                                   │
│  Hibernate AUTO FLUSH                                     │
│       │                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                      │
│  │ Compare entity snapshot         │                      │
│  │ Generate UPDATE/INSERT SQL      │                      │
│  │ Send to database                │                      │
│  └─────────────────────────────────┘                      │
│       │                                                   │
│  Data persisted ✓                                         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  FlushMode.MANUAL (readOnly=true)                         │
│                                                           │
│  Entity modified → dirty flag set (ignored)               │
│       │                                                   │
│  Before query or commit:                                  │
│       │                                                   │
│  Hibernate SKIPS flush                                    │
│       │                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                      │
│  │ No snapshot comparison          │                      │
│  │ No SQL generated                │                      │
│  │ Nothing sent to database        │                      │
│  └─────────────────────────────────┘                      │
│       │                                                   │
│  Transaction commits (read-only)                          │
│  Pending changes DISCARDED silently                       │
│  Data NOT persisted ✗                                     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The reason @Transactional(readOnly=true) can make a write silently disappear is that Spring uses it to switch the Hibernate session's flush mode to MANUAL. Normally, Hibernate runs in AUTO flush mode, so before a query and at commit time it automatically generates INSERT and UPDATE statements from the in-memory persistence context. Under readOnly, the flush mode is MANUAL, which means that automatic flush never happens. Any entity modification or save() call stays in memory and is quietly discarded when the transaction commits. There is no exception and no warning.

At the National Bank of India, a developer put readOnly=true on the entire AccountService class because most methods were lookups and read-only transactions are a genuine performance optimization. The problem was that the transfer() and createAccount() methods inherited that readOnly setting. They debited and credited entities in memory, returned success, and committed nothing. Priya was told her transfer succeeded, but the money never moved. The code looked correct and even passed shallow tests because the in-memory entity objects had the correct values.

Pankaj, the architect, enforces a strict rule: readOnly=true is placed only on individual query methods, never at the class level of a service that also writes. If a class-level default must exist, every write method gets an explicit @Transactional override. In code review, any write operation under an inherited readOnly is treated as a severity P0 bug.

Remember one sentence: readOnly=true is a correctness switch disguised as a performance optimization -- it silently drops writes, so never let a write method inherit it.
